linux.mechanism: allowlisted /proc/sys reads (open/read, errno-classified absent/unreadable; a missing key is absent only when statfs confirms its nearest existing directory is procfs)

windows.fallback: Rig-verified 2026-09-21: MitigationOptions/MitigationAuditOptions are ABSENT on a default Windows 11 install (rows read `absent`, not a failure); a present value decodes as 16 two-bit nibbles (dep, sehop, aslr_bottom_up, aslr_high_entropy and cfg confirmed on hardware); GetProcessMitigationPolicy succeeds for DEP/ASLR/CFG on x64.

caveats: **No documented business driver.** The priority for this plugin is asserted from a capability-gap reading, not evidenced by any tracked demand (see "How it works"); there is no capability-map requirement, named customer, SOC 2 control or CVE behind it (the capability-map row lists the plugin; it does not drive it).

**Two state vocabularies.** Linux and macOS report `enabled`/`disabled`/`partial`, while Windows reports `on`/`off`/`default` because a system-wide mitigation nibble is a tri-state override, not a hardening level, so consumers key on the `<os>` column. The three non-value states (`unmodelled`, `absent`, `unreadable`) are the same on every OS.

**`absent` does not downgrade the run, and is only reported where the surface is confirmed present.** A missing optional key (no Yama, no `MitigationOptions` on a default Windows install) adds no token and the run stays `OK`, while a hidden Linux surface or a missing Windows `Session Manager\kernel` key reads `unreadable` instead (see "How it works"). The one exception is the Linux backstop: all eleven keys `absent` on a confirmed procfs adds `proc_sys:not_visible` and reports `CONSTRAINED`.

**Windows: the self rows are the agent process only, and only part of the mitigation layout is hardware-confirmed.** The `self.*` rows come from `GetProcessMitigationPolicy` on the agent's own process; the system-wide policy is the `mitigation.*` registry rows. Only five of the sixteen nibble positions (`dep`, `sehop`, `aslr_bottom_up`, `aslr_high_entropy`, `cfg`) and nibble value `1` were confirmed on the-rig (2026-09-21); the other positions and values, trailing `ext_q<n>` QWORDs, every `MitigationAuditOptions` row, a `REG_QWORD` value and Windows on ARM64 (x64 emulation) are unmeasured.

**Fixed allowlists, no discovery; a container reads the kernel the agent runs on.** The plugin reads only the keys listed above, so it does not report Linux LSM state (SELinux, AppArmor) or macOS SIP and Gatekeeper posture. The Linux keys are kernel-global, so a containerised agent (including the shipped `deploy/docker/Dockerfile.agent` image, where the Linux sample was captured) reports the kernel it runs on: the host's under a shared-kernel runtime such as runc, the guest kernel's under Kata or a microVM, and under gVisor a synthetic procfs that may implement only some of the keys (unmeasured here; the rest would read `absent`).

definitions.description: Reports one row per allowlisted exploit-mitigation or kernel-hardening key: which OS, which key, the raw value read, and a state token. Linux reads eleven /proc/sys keys, macOS four sysctl keys, Windows the system-wide mitigation registry values plus the agent process's own DEP/ASLR/CFG policy. A key that does not exist on this host reads `absent`, which is a normal answer and not a failure; a key that exists but could not be read reads `unreadable` and downgrades the result to CONSTRAINED/PARTIAL (PERMISSION_DENIED/PARTIAL when the read was refused) rather than failing the command. A not-found only reads `absent` where the surface itself is confirmed present: on Linux a hidden or unmounted /proc/sys makes every key `unreadable`, and on Windows a missing Session Manager\kernel key (present on every install) reads `unreadable`. One Linux backstop is not a key's own row: all eleven keys `absent` on a confirmed procfs adds the reason `proc_sys:not_visible` and reports CONSTRAINED/PARTIAL with every row still `absent`. In a container the Linux keys are those of the kernel the agent runs on (the host's under a shared-kernel runtime).

how_it_works:
One action, `posture` (`system_hardening_plugin.cpp`), reads a fixed allowlist of exploit-mitigation and kernel-hardening keys and writes one row per key: `posture|<os>|<key>|<raw>|<state>`. The action takes no parameters, so no request text ever reaches a path or a registry name. Every leg is rung 1 and never spawns a process. The allowlists are:

- **Linux** (`/proc/sys`, opened read-only and non-blocking with `open`, checked with `fstat`, then `read` only if it is a regular file; one table of key to path, no directory walk): `kernel.randomize_va_space`, `kernel.kptr_restrict`, `kernel.yama.ptrace_scope`, `kernel.dmesg_restrict`, `kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled`, `kernel.sysrq`, `fs.protected_hardlinks`, `fs.protected_symlinks`, `fs.protected_fifos`, `fs.protected_regular`, `fs.suid_dumpable`.
- **macOS** (`sysctlbyname`): `kern.securelevel`, `kern.coredump`, `kern.sugid_coredump`, `kern.bootargs`. `kern.nx` is deliberately not read: it is an unknown oid on Apple Silicon.
- **Windows** (registry plus one API): the `MitigationOptions` and `MitigationAuditOptions` values under `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\kernel` (a `REG_BINARY`, or an 8-byte `REG_QWORD` as Microsoft's documented untrusted-font-blocking steps write it; any other type or size reads `unreadable`, `<name>:type_<n>`), decoded per policy into `mitigation.<policy>` and `mitigation_audit.<policy>` rows (DEP, SEHOP, force-relocate, bottom-up and high-entropy ASLR, CFG and the other fields of the kernel's system-wide mitigation option map, one two-bit nibble per policy), and `GetProcessMitigationPolicy` on the agent's own process for the `self.*` rows (DEP, ASLR, CFG). Only the agent's own process is queried; no other process is enumerated.

Every key reads as exactly one of three things: a **value** (with a state), **`absent`** (the OS definitively reports the key is not there), or **`unreadable`** (the read failed). A failed read never reads as absent: the errno (Linux, macOS) or Win32 error (Windows) decides. A not-found only counts as absence where the surface being read is itself known to be present:

- **Linux.** An `ENOENT` is `absent` only when `statfs` confirms the key's nearest existing directory up to `/proc/sys` is a mounted procfs (`surface_is_procfs`, in the pure header). If that confirmation probe finds no procfs, `remap_enoent_for_surface` turns the `ENOENT` into `ENODEV` and the key reads `unreadable` with `<key>:errno_19`. If the confirmation probe itself is refused (`EACCES`/`EPERM` on an ancestor `statfs` — a seccomp profile or an LSM that splits `open` from `statfs`), that refusal is never downgraded to `ENODEV`: it reports `unreadable` with `<key>:eacces` like any other denial. Measured 2026-09-23 in a container: a tmpfs over `/proc/sys`, and a `subset=pid` procfs, each gave eleven `errno_19` rows and `CONSTRAINED`/`PARTIAL`; a tmpfs over `/proc/sys/kernel` made only the six `kernel.*` keys `unreadable`. A leaf that opens but is not a regular file (a FIFO, device or directory mounted at the path) is never read and reports `unreadable` with `<key>:not_regular`.
- **Windows.** A not-found registry VALUE is `absent`, but a not-found `Session Manager\kernel` KEY, which exists on every install, reads `unreadable` with `<name>:key_missing` (`ReadSource::structural_key`). From `GetProcessMitigationPolicy`, `ERROR_NOT_SUPPORTED` is `absent`, while `ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER` reads `unreadable` with `<name>:win32_87`: every supported target (Windows 10+ x64) implements the DEP, ASLR and CFG policies, so it can only mean a malformed call.

Absence is not a failure: an `absent` row adds no reason token and does not lower the result status, so a host that lacks an optional key (a default Windows install, which has no `MitigationOptions`, or a Linux kernel without Yama) reports `OK`. Each `unreadable` row carries one reason token. The one token that belongs to no row is the Linux backstop `proc_sys:not_visible`: all eleven keys `ENOENT` on a confirmed procfs keeps every row `absent` but reports `CONSTRAINED`. On Linux and macOS the state is `enabled`, `disabled` or `partial`, describing the hardening rather than the raw number (`kernel.sysrq=0` is `enabled`, `kern.coredump=1` is `disabled`); `unmodelled` means a value was read that the table has no interpretation for. A Linux value is judged whole (whitespace trimmed from both ends), never on its first line. Windows uses `on`, `off` and `default` instead, because a system-wide mitigation nibble is a tri-state override (not set, always on, always off) and not a hardening level. An empty macOS `kern.bootargs` is a successful read of an empty string, not a failure. Emptiness is judged on the whole value with whitespace and NULs trimmed, so a value such as `"\n-v"` is `unmodelled`, not `enabled`, and the raw column carries all of it.

**Threat-model boundary (Linux).** The surface gate detects a hidden or replaced `/proc/sys`; it does not defend against an actor with root or `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` in the agent's mount namespace, who can bind a real procfs directory or a forged regular file over a key (the value then reads as that file says) or mount a filesystem that never answers (an unresponsive FUSE daemon) so the read blocks. A FIFO or device placed at a key path is handled: it reads `unreadable` with `<key>:not_regular` without blocking.

**Why this plugin exists (stated plainly, not inflated).** Zero documented driver: no capability-map *requirement*, enterprise-parity, SOC 2 or `docs/roadmap.md` entry names this plugin as a need (the capability-map plugin-inventory row is added by this change as a listing, not a driver); the nearest adjacent doc idea (`docs/roadmap.md` Issue 18.2 "Compliance Reporting Templates," CIS-benchmark-shaped) is a reporting/templating layer over rules that would already have to exist elsewhere, not a justification for this collection plugin itself, and is itself only "Proposed." This is pure capability-gap reasoning, not evidenced demand.
name: system_hardening

columns.description: Row family: `posture` (one per allowlisted key) or `constrained` (an internal-error row: `os` is the host leg, `key` is `internal_error`, `state` is `unreadable`).
columns.name: row_kind

columns.description: The leg that produced the row.
columns.name: os

columns.description: Allowlisted key: a sysctl name (Linux, macOS) or a policy name (Windows: mitigation.<policy> and mitigation_audit.<policy> from the registry, self.<policy> from the agent process; a registry value that was not decoded (absent or unreadable) reports under mitigation_options or mitigation_audit_options, and a failed self policy under self.dep, self.aslr or self.cfg; the trailing QWORDs of a longer registry blob appear as ext_q<n> rows).
columns.name: key

columns.description: The raw value read (integer, string, or 0x-prefixed hex on Windows); "-" when nothing was read (absent or unreadable). An empty macOS kern.bootargs is a successful read and an empty column.
columns.name: raw

columns.description: Linux and macOS: enabled/disabled/partial describe the hardening (enabled = protection on, partial = on at a weaker level), not the sysctl value. Windows: on/off/default, because a system-wide mitigation nibble is a tri-state override (not set / always on / always off), not a hardening level. unmodelled = a value was read that this table has no interpretation for. absent = the key does not exist here (only where the surface being read is confirmed present). unreadable = the read failed, or the surface itself (a hidden /proc/sys, a missing Session Manager\kernel key) was not there.
columns.name: state

outputs_note: Pipe-delimited rows, one per allowlisted key, in allowlist order, written via `write_output()`. The first field is the fixed literal `posture`, then `<os>`, `<key>`, `<raw>` and `<state>`. `<raw>` is `-` when nothing was read (`absent` or `unreadable`); a raw value that WAS read passes through the shared untrusted-output escaper, with newlines and NULs folded to spaces so no value can split or cut a row. A Windows value that was not decoded (absent or unreadable) reports one row under its registry row name, `mitigation_options` or `mitigation_audit_options`, and a failed self policy one row under `self.dep`, `self.aslr` or `self.cfg`. Windows rows can outnumber the allowlist: one registry value decodes into one row per policy field, and each trailing QWORD of a longer blob adds one raw-hex `ext_q<n>` row (`default` when zero, otherwise `unmodelled`) rather than being dropped. The action returns 0 for every data-level outcome (an unreadable key is a degraded result and an absent key is not a failure; neither is ever a failed command); only an internal exception returns 1 (any leg), adding a `constrained|<os>|internal_error|-|unreadable` row (the same five fields as every other row) after any rows already written. A value that was read but cannot be interpreted is `unmodelled` (Linux and macOS: non-numeric, empty or out-of-range text; Windows: a nibble with no modelled meaning), while a Windows blob whose structure cannot be decoded at all (empty, odd length, not QWORD-aligned, oversized) is `unreadable` with a reason token.

privileges.if_refused: `ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND`/`ERROR_PATH_NOT_FOUND` on a registry value reports that row `absent` with no token (the default state of a fresh install), as does `ERROR_NOT_SUPPORTED` from `GetProcessMitigationPolicy` for that `self.*` row; `ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER` from `GetProcessMitigationPolicy` reports it `unreadable` with `<name>:win32_87` (every supported target implements the three policies, so it is a malformed call, not an answer); an `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` reports it `unreadable` with reason `<name>:access_denied` and the action reports `PERMISSION_DENIED`/`PARTIAL`; any other Win32 error reports `unreadable` with `<name>:win32_<n>`. A not-found on the `Session Manager\kernel` key itself (not a value inside it) reports both registry rows `unreadable` with `<name>:key_missing` and the action reports `CONSTRAINED`/`PARTIAL`: that key exists on every install, so its absence is never a clean answer
privileges.measured: 2026-09-21, bare-metal, the-rig (Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26200), `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM` — real capture (`docs/samples/windows.txt`); the mitigation probe summary is in the `system_hardening_win.cpp` banner

privileges.grant: None — `sysctlbyname` reads of these keys are unprivileged
privileges.if_refused: `EPERM` reports the key `unreadable` with reason `<key>:eacces` and the action reports `PERMISSION_DENIED`/`PARTIAL`; an unknown oid (`ENOENT`) reports it `absent` with no token and leaves the result unchanged
privileges.measured: 2026-09-23, bare-metal, this Mac (`braga`), unprivileged (euid 501) — real capture (`docs/samples/macos.txt`); no root-privileged run has been captured, so the root identity above is the documented production default, not a measured one
privileges.runs_as: agent daemon, root today (LaunchDaemon carries no `UserName` key — `docs/agent-privilege-model.md` TL;DR); this plugin's reads need no elevation beyond that default

privileges.grant: None — the allowlisted `/proc/sys` files are world-readable on current kernels. On older kernels the four `fs.protected_*` files were root-only (mode 0600), so a non-root agent there reads them `unreadable` (`<key>:eacces`) and the action reports `PERMISSION_DENIED`; that is from kernel history and was not measured here
privileges.if_refused: `EACCES`/`EPERM` reports the key `unreadable` with reason `<key>:eacces` and the action reports `PERMISSION_DENIED`/`PARTIAL`; a leaf that is not a regular file reports `unreadable` with `<key>:not_regular`; any other errno reports `unreadable` with `<key>:errno_<n>`; a missing file (`ENOENT`, for example `kernel.yama.ptrace_scope` with Yama not built in) reports it `absent` with no token and leaves the result unchanged, but only once `statfs` confirms the nearest existing directory above it (up to `/proc/sys`) is a mounted procfs; if that directory is not procfs (`/proc/sys` hidden by `ProcSubset=pid`, masked, overmounted or unmounted in a container) the `ENOENT` is remapped to `ENODEV` and the key reads `unreadable` with `<key>:errno_19` — unless the confirmation `statfs` was itself refused (`EACCES`/`EPERM`), in which case it is never downgraded to `ENODEV`: the key reads `unreadable` with `<key>:eacces` and the action reports `PERMISSION_DENIED`, same as a refused leaf. As a backstop, if ALL ELEVEN keys read `ENOENT` on a confirmed procfs, one additional `proc_sys:not_visible` token downgrades the result to `CONSTRAINED` (each row still reads `absent`)
privileges.measured: 2026-09-23, container (Docker VM on this Mac), root (`euid 0`), plus the refused-leaf, tmpfs-overmount and `subset=pid` probes — a real live capture of the built `.so` (`docs/samples/linux.txt`). Separately, all ten keys present on kernel 7.0 were measured world-readable (mode 0644) by a non-root user (uid 65534) in a container

result_status.when: No key was `unreadable`: every key was either read or `absent`, except that all eleven Linux keys `absent` on a confirmed procfs is the `proc_sys:not_visible` backstop (`CONSTRAINED`, next row). An absent key adds no reason token, so a host that lacks an optional key (Yama not built into the Linux kernel, `MitigationOptions` never written on a default Windows install) still reports `OK`.

At least one key was `unreadable`, or the Linux backstop fired, and none was refused. The reason lists one `<key>:<cause>` token per unreadable key, whose row reads `unreadable`; `proc_sys:not_visible` alone means all eleven Linux keys read `absent` on a confirmed procfs, with no `unreadable` row. Windows decoder failures (`empty_blob`, `odd_length`, `not_qword_aligned`, `oversized`) appear as `<name>:<token>`.
Any leg: an unexpected exception escaped a leg and was contained in `execute()`; the action returns 1 with the row `constrained|<os>|internal_error|-|unreadable`.

Any leg: a read was refused — `EACCES`/`EPERM` on Linux and macOS (token `<key>:eacces`) or `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` on Windows (token `<name>:access_denied`). A refusal outranks every other unreadable cause in the same run; the reason still lists every unreadable key's token.

where_the_data_goes: **Instruction result.** Rows travel over the agent's mTLS gRPC channel as the command response and land in the ResponseStore, queryable at `/api/responses/{id}`. `posture` is also a gathered definition (`crossplatform.system_hardening.posture`, 300s TTL).
**Not consumed by** daily-sync, TAR, DEX, or metrics.

**Sensitivity.** Rows carry kernel and mitigation settings only: no username, path, process name or installed-software name. The values are a security-posture baseline of the host (for example ASLR off, ptrace unrestricted, core dumps enabled), which is useful to an attacker choosing an exploit, so the rows warrant the same handling as other `Security` data. `kern.bootargs`, where non-empty, echoes the host's whole boot-argument string (newlines and NULs shown as spaces).

**Siblings:** `vuln_scan` (its configuration checks read two of the same Linux keys, `kernel.randomize_va_space` and `fs.suid_dumpable`, as pass/fail findings; this plugin reports the raw value and state) and `bitlocker` (disk encryption posture).
